days.title: Tools of Genetic Engineering
days.content:
🎯 Learning Objectives

  • Identify the tools used in genetic engineering.
  • Describe restriction enzymes.
  • Explain the role of plasmids and vectors.
  • Describe DNA ligase and gel electrophoresis.

🔑 Key Concepts

  • Restriction enzyme — cuts DNA at specific sequences.
  • Plasmid — circular DNA vector.
  • DNA ligase — seals DNA fragments.
  • Gel electrophoresis — separates DNA by size.

📚 Lesson Content

A. Tools of Genetic Engineering

ToolFunction
Restriction enzymeCuts DNA at specific sites
DNA ligaseSeals DNA fragments together
PlasmidCarrier/vector for DNA
Gel electrophoresisSeparates fragments by size
PCRAmplifies DNA

B. Why Restriction Enzymes?

They produce sticky ends that allow complementary base pairing — essential for building recombinant DNA.

scenarios.text: An enzyme cuts DNA at GAATTC.
Two DNA fragments are joined together.
A circular DNA is used to carry a gene.
DNA fragments are separated by size.
A small DNA sample is amplified millions of times.
DNA fragments have overhanging single-stranded ends.

questions.text: Which enzyme cuts DNA at specific sequences?
Which molecule is used as a vector in gene cloning?

takeaways: Restriction enzymes cut DNA at specific sequences.
PCR amplifies DNA; gel electrophoresis separates fragments.

days.title: Steps in Creating Recombinant DNA
days.content:
🎯 Learning Objectives

  • Outline the steps in creating recombinant DNA.
  • Explain gene cloning.
  • Describe transformation of bacteria.
  • Explain selection of successful recombinants.

🔑 Key Concepts

  • Recombinant DNA — DNA combining sequences from different sources.
  • Transformation — uptake of foreign DNA by bacteria.
  • Selection — identifying bacteria that took up the plasmid.
  • Gene cloning — producing many copies of a gene.

📚 Lesson Content

A. Steps in Creating Recombinant DNA

  1. Isolate gene of interest
  2. Cut plasmid with same restriction enzyme
  3. Ligate gene into plasmid
  4. Introduce plasmid into bacteria (transformation)
  5. Select successful recombinants
  6. Grow bacteria — they produce the gene product

B. Example: Human Insulin

The human insulin gene is inserted into E. coli plasmids. Bacteria produce insulin, which is harvested and purified.

scenarios.text: A gene is cut out of human DNA.
A plasmid is cut with the same enzyme.
Ligase joins gene and plasmid.
Bacteria take up the plasmid.
Antibiotic resistance identifies successful recombinants.
Bacteria grow and produce insulin.

questions.text: What is the FIRST step in creating recombinant DNA?
Which enzyme joins the gene to the plasmid?

takeaways: Steps: isolate gene → cut plasmid → ligate → transform → select → grow.
Restriction enzymes create matching sticky ends.

days.title: Applications of Recombinant DNA
days.content:
🎯 Learning Objectives

  • Identify real-world applications of recombinant DNA.
  • Describe medical applications.
  • Describe agricultural applications.
  • Explain industrial uses.

🔑 Key Concepts

  • Medicine — insulin, vaccines, gene therapy.
  • Agriculture — pest-resistant crops, Golden Rice.
  • Industry — enzymes, biofuels.
  • Research — gene function studies.

📚 Lesson Content

A. Medical Applications

  • Human insulin for diabetes
  • Human growth hormone
  • Hepatitis B vaccine
  • Gene therapy

B. Agricultural Applications

  • Bt corn (pest-resistant)
  • Golden Rice (Vitamin A)
  • Herbicide-resistant soybeans
  • Drought-tolerant crops

C. Industrial Applications

  • Enzymes for detergents and food
  • Biofuels from engineered microbes
  • Bioremediation of pollutants

scenarios.text: Diabetics use bacterially-produced insulin.
A corn plant produces its own pesticide.
Rice is enriched with beta-carotene.
Bacteria digest oil spills.
A vaccine is produced using yeast.
A gene therapy treats a genetic disorder.

questions.text: Bt corn is an example of:
Which is a medical application of recombinant DNA?

takeaways: Recombinant DNA benefits medicine, agriculture, and industry.

days.title: Ethical Issues & Future Directions
days.content:
🎯 Learning Objectives

  • Identify ethical issues in genetic engineering.
  • Discuss pros and cons of GMOs.
  • Describe future directions in biotechnology.
  • Analyze bioethical dilemmas.

🔑 Key Concepts

  • Bioethics — ethics of biological research.
  • GMO — genetically modified organism.
  • CRISPR — gene editing tool.
  • Gene therapy — correcting genetic disorders.

📚 Lesson Content

A. Ethical Concerns

  • Safety of GMO foods
  • Environmental impact (gene flow)
  • Designer babies
  • Privacy of genetic information
  • Access and cost of gene therapies

B. Future Directions

  • CRISPR-based therapies
  • Personalized medicine
  • Engineered organs
  • Synthetic biology

C. Balanced View

Recombinant DNA technology has transformed medicine, agriculture, and industry. Responsible use requires oversight, transparency, and ethical review.

scenarios.text: A GMO crop could spread genes to wild plants.
A couple wants to select their baby's traits.
A person's genetic info could be used against them.
CRISPR corrects a mutation causing a disease.
Gene therapy is expensive and not accessible to all.
GMO foods are extensively tested before release.

questions.text: What is a major ethical concern about GMOs?
Which is a future direction of genetic engineering?

takeaways: GMO concerns include safety, environment, and equity.
Future directions: personalized medicine, engineered organs.
